newsitem.title: USA: Group calls for appointed Cleveland school board.
newsitem.headline: Group calls for appointed Cleveland school board.

text.p: A group studying the governance of the Cleveland City School District recommended Wednesday that the district be run by a board appointed by the city's mayor.

The Advisory Committee on Governance of the Cleveland Summit on Education urged legislators to amend state law to allow the mayor to appoint a nine-member board of education, with the mayor serving as chairman of the board.

"The time has come for radical change in the way our school district is governed -- tinkering around the edges will not work. The district needs a governing body that can deal with issues creatively, effectively and immediately," said a report released Wednesday by the group.
The report recommended a pilot program that would begin next year, followed by a district-wide vote on a binding referendum in 2001.
Cleveland Mayor Michael White had no immediate reaction to the report, according to a spokeswoman.

A bill has already been introduced in the Ohio Legislature giving Cleveland's mayor power over the school system. Bill Wendling, an adviser to the governance committee, said the group hopes legislators will take the report into account as they refine the bill.
The group's report said the time has come to try a new approach to governing Cleveland schools.

"The elected board of education structure has failed to meet its responsibilities up to now," said a news release from the group. "The (elected) board has allowed itself to be shackled by quibbling over day-to-day management issues while ignoring the broader governance issues of student achievement, leadership, planning and goal setting, and parent and community involvement."
The report also noted the district has made "remarkable progress," since the state took it over in March 1995.

Since that time, the district has completed and begun to implement a comprehensive long-range strategic plan, entered into a three-year contract with the teacher's union, and passed a federal court-ordered 13.5 mill property tax levy in November.
In October, the Ohio auditor declared the district to be in a fiscal emergency as a result of a financial crisis that included a fiscal 1997 operating deficit of $89.5 million.
